objections.objection: The recommendation (at least 15.5 kWh) comes after three sections of calculation. One reading says the sizing figure could have come first. The better reading is that the load, autonomy and derating steps are the method that produces the answer and are needed to interpret it, so they are not unnecessary run-up.

The survey of methods mentions alcohol spray, which the recommendation later uses, so it could be read as context for the choice. But most of it is generic (ozone, UV, freezing, sustainability targets) and adds little to understanding the specific recommendation.

The recommendation comes after an evaluation of the options. Each option section reports site-specific test results or constraints that rule that option out and explain why the duplicate-jacket plan was chosen, so it is meaningful reasoning, not filler. A stricter reading would expect a recommendation report to put its conclusion first.

The opening 'short answer' only repeats what the asker says they already know (rotate groups). The numbers they actually asked for come after two paragraphs of memoir, Leeuwenhoek history and a survey on the value of practicals, none of which helps interpret those numbers. A reader could treat the opener as an early summary, but it does not answer the stated task.

The rotation is stated in the third paragraph, but the two paragraphs before it split the practical into its two jobs, give the median timings and work out the time budget. That is the causal reasoning the staggered schedule depends on, so the answer comes later without being buried.

The committee's stopwatch counts and questionnaire play no part in the answer, because the text later says planning consent settled the location before the survey. One could read this as context for the members, but it is a methodology tour that delays the stated answer.

The grant administration and plywood history do not help interpret the clamping recommendation. The note about the grant's oversight could arguably explain why the Committee is involved, but the history of plywood and bent furniture is unrelated run-up before the recommendation.

The answer and its qualification come in the first paragraph ('In brief: the main layover moves to the new turning loop'). The later Market Square history is a digression that comes after the answer, so it may belong to another check but is not a buried answer.

The recommendation comes after three paragraphs, but those paragraphs set out the adhesive, pressure and equipment constraints, and each one rules out an otherwise obvious method. This is necessary reasoning the text says it is giving on purpose, not unnecessary run-up.

The water temperatures arrive in the fourth paragraph. Everything before them is causal reasoning the answer depends on: why the proof needs no stagger, why levain is ruled out, and the per-degree bulk arithmetic. That is necessary setup, not unnecessary run-up.

Competing reading: the Monday-levain section is useful advice on a separate topic, so it could be classed as an off-topic aside rather than an organization defect. It still comes between the stated stagger question and its answer, and it does nothing to help interpret the proof-temperature split, so it meets the delay requirement.

The decision comes after four paragraphs. Each one is a prerequisite the allocation depends on: attendance versus bookings, per-lane capacity limits, the demand calculation showing 10 lanes needed for 8, and the failed alternating-weeks trial that rules out one option. All of this is necessary reasoning, not filler.

The sentence about catalog-only versus row-rewriting changes is relevant, but the question has already said which change is which, so it adds little. The generic definitions of migration and nightly import contribute nothing to interpreting the answer.

The last sentence of the club-history paragraph, about each club feeling it has a claim, touches on the dispute. Even so, the building history, the author's personal memories and the club founding stories don't help interpret the lane allocation, and they delay it by three paragraphs.

One paragraph, the soak-rig voltage, flow, bearing and load-cell figures, could count as relevant elimination of other causes. But the text frames those checks as protocol logging, and the intake, bulletin and case-review material clearly delays the diagnosis without contributing to it.

The explicit verdict ('The washer does not need repairing') comes late. However, the material before it is purposeful diagnostic reasoning: separating the three possible causes, the pump tests, the fault-time log and the reproduction. That is necessary causal evidence, and 'The pump looks healthy' gives an early partial answer.

One reading treats the lab-scoring paragraph as a needed prerequisite, since knowing how pairs are scored explains why the samples should be identical. Against that, the reporting limits, the absolute-agreement rule, last spring's copper values and the D3 qualifier do not inform the spacing answer. The rationale actually given afterwards (repeatability on identical water) stands without them.

There are two ways to read this. Under the stricter reading, the Background is a generic tutorial and history lesson for a committee the text says has already polar-aligned mounts, so it adds nothing to understanding the recommendation and delays it. Under the more lenient reading, separating polar alignment from star alignment is a definition the recommendation relies on, so that part could count as necessary setup. Even so, the Fraunhofer history and the precession detail contribute nothing.

The decision comes after three sections on the link, the tests and the codec. Those sections give the causal evidence the slot choice depends on: congestion windows, tide-linked burst outages and the codec's burst tolerance. The note also says up front why it is ordered this way. That makes it necessary reasoning, not unnecessary run-up. A reader who expects decision notes to lead with the decision could still see this as delay.

Part of the signal-chain material (the app-to-codec path) touches on why a live slot is risky. However, the STL retirement, the transmitter fallback, the data bill and the dump/rebuild behaviour add nothing to interpreting the scheduling decision, which comes only after all of it.

The run-up is a single paragraph on a related swap topic (rotor rub). One reading treats it as a sibling digression, closer to off-topic content than burial. The other reading counts it as unrelated explanation that delays the stated answer, since it contributes nothing to understanding the indexing procedure.

The timed walk from the tram stop and the 2023 Durham comparison are loosely relevant to arrivals. But the WiFi, socket, ceiling-height, acoustics and catering material has nothing to do with queuing, and it comes before the recommendation.

The early 'In brief' summary looks like an answer, but it doesn't settle either decision that was asked for (folded or opened; what goes between the faces). It works as a teaser. The actual answers come only after the provenance, team-history, transport-risk and tender material.

The answers come late, but the memo says up front that both depend on the 2019 journey. The hinge, logger, resonance and cushion-curve material is the causal reasoning that leads to the answers, not unnecessary run-up.

The four-table recommendation comes after three paragraphs of figures. The writer says in advance that the answer depends on those numbers, and each one is used directly to choose the table count and where the queue goes. The key point that no checking happens at the door also appears early.

One could argue the $100 two-signature purchase rule bears slightly on the $84 price. But the handover of the coordinator role, the donation history and the regional trends add nothing to understanding the recommendation.

The explicit recommendation comes late, but the earlier material is the sightline arithmetic that shows why height is the wrong fix, so it is necessary causal reasoning. The opening also signals the answer early: raising the board is not the solution.

Briefing notes usually include background, and the paragraph on testing consolidation during the closure is loosely related to having a single temporary stop. Even so, the consolidation history, late-running enforcement and works-timing correspondence add little to the stop-location answer, which only arrives in section 2.

The recommendation is held back until section 4. But the note says early that it rejects the contractor's location, and the Calder Road evidence and the conditions derived from it are necessary causal reasoning for a choice that is not obvious from a map, so the order is purposeful.

The decision comes after three paragraphs, but those paragraphs are the throughput arithmetic and the CPU and connection-pool limits that the chosen value of 5 per host is derived from. That is meaningful methodology, not run-up. One competing reading is that decision records conventionally lead with the decision, but the position of the answer alone does not establish a defect.

The text says early that the answer depends on what is failing. The diagnosis that follows (board creep rather than hardware failure, and the span arithmetic) is the causal basis for recommending repair over replacement, so it is necessary reasoning, not delay.

One competing reading is that the paragraphs on timber movement and finish are a diagnostic step that rules out the wood before naming the fixings as the cause. The text never presents them that way, though, and they don't connect to the tilt. They read as general background that delays "The tilt comes from the fixings."

The run-up is only one paragraph, and someone could read it as investigative methodology that rules out flour and slicer causes. But the text never draws on the flour figures, blade tension or dough temperatures. The answer rests entirely on core temperature and starch set, so the paragraph reads as self-narration that delays the answer.

The recommendation comes after four constraint sections, so a reader who wants the answer first might call it buried. Each constraint directly narrows the interval to 14 or 28 days, though, so the run-up is necessary causal reasoning in a deliberate order, not unnecessary material.

The run-up is only one paragraph. The opening already states the governing principle (pixels per inch at print size), and the dpi-versus-ppi note gives the reader some context. Even so, the etymology and history of the word 'pixel' add nothing to the answer, and the operative figures are held back behind that background.

Because the household has just moved, the advice on letting a fridge settle could count as related context. But the writer says outright that the asker's fridge cools fine and that the section is unrelated to the rattle, so it is a detour before the answer.

The detailed proposal comes late, but the opening answers the first question ('It should not'). It also says the constraints are set out first because they determine what replaces the queue, and the queue failure, device differences and capacity figures all feed directly into the proposal. That makes it purposefully ordered reasoning, not burial.

The combi-fan paragraph is somewhat relevant because it notes uneven browning across trays. Still, the Maillard and sugar-content background does little to explain the holding plan, which comes only after it.

One reading treats "How we got here" as the decision record's meaningful method section. But the parcels desk's rule decided the question ("That settles it"), and the consultations, bike-bay measurements and show of hands contribute little to understanding the answer.

The exposure numbers come in the fourth paragraph, but the mount drift limits and the target pixel scale are prerequisites. They directly set the 10-second and 6-second values and the decision to drop Saturn, so this setup is necessary rather than unnecessary.

The decision comes after the operator rules, the measurements and the connection timing. Each section is causal reasoning the decision relies on: the box jams at the aisle turn, there's no time to repack, and the branch train has only unreserved space. Some might want a decision note to lead with the decision, but this setup is necessary rather than unnecessary.

The opening already narrows the fault to 'at or below that outlet,' which could be read as an early summary. However, it is only a partial answer. The operative answer, roots in the buried drain line, comes after a generic gutter history and profile tour that does not help interpret it.

The directive ('So: do not leave either piece in Corley Hall past Thursday night') appears late. Every preceding step is still needed to interpret it: the two-device distinction, the work-order power cutoff, and the 101-hour gap. This is purposefully ordered causal reasoning, not burial.

The answer ('overshoot from the valley') comes only under Recommendation. Before it come a definitions section and a long measurement section, which one could read as a delayed answer. But the three overflow types are necessary to interpret 'overshoot, not spill-over,' and the hose test, camera, storm film and capacity check are meaningful methodology. They rule out the competing causes and support the secondary item.

The 50 lux answer arrives in the fourth paragraph. The material before it (illuminance versus dose, the sensitivity category, the lit-hours arithmetic) is causal reasoning that the setting and rest period depend on. It is needed setup, not run-up.

The opening incident paragraph is needed context. The Background section (fuel curves, wet stacking, tank and filter details) does nothing to explain the changeover steps, and the text itself says it is not in question. It delays the requested procedure.

The procedure comes after three findings sections, but the text says each finding changes a step. The UPS gap, freezer restart delay and bonding issue each set a step or a hardware choice in the procedure, so this is a necessary prerequisite.

The opening incident paragraph is relevant setup. The gloss-versus-matte printing aside has nothing to do with moving the boards, and it delays the trolley plan. A competing reading is that it is a short, signalled aside in a club notice; it is still an unrelated preliminary placed before the answer.

The answer (4 bikes on the 07:40, 8 on the 08:20, no booking) comes only in the penultimate paragraph. However, the material before it (space vs time, dwell timing, peak loads, the two-places-per-bike rule) is the calculation that produces those caps, so it reads as necessary reasoning rather than unnecessary run-up. A competing reading would expect the caps to be stated up front.

The early 'short version' (keep the length comparison, use the new stands) could be read as an early summary. But the task Dr Keane set is the lengths, release angle and timing method, and those are withheld until after history, memoir and forum material that contributes nothing to interpreting them.
The boarding-time data and crew views are loosely relevant context. But the decision rests entirely on the Corran's gangway gradient, so the methodology tour adds little to interpreting the answer.

Competing reading: a multi-finding field-service report may legitimately cover former, retarder and flour issues. But the text sets out only the mixer-order question and puts these unrelated findings (one is explicitly 'nothing to do with' the mix) before that answer, so I read it as burial.

The working offset formula only arrives in the third answer paragraph. Still, the opening paragraph already splits the error into a fixed one-hour part and a drift of 1.0 s/day. The physics check that follows is what justifies using a linear model, so it is meaningful methodology, not empty run-up.

The recommendation comes after a long options review, but that review isn't filler. Lantern's two-tag limit, Option A's failure on existing owners, and the stranded ISBN reviews are exactly what the tiered design depends on. Briefing order with purposeful reasoning rather than burial.

Survey-of-practice background in a committee briefing could be read as deliberate context. Here it is generic: it never feeds into the banner-over-replica recommendation, which rests only on PressFrame's capabilities and archive integrity.

The decision comes after three sections of setup. Each section is a constraint the decision depends on: degraded cycle throughput, the items needed twice and their deadlines, and the closed 19:15–19:50 window. This is necessary causal setup, not unnecessary run-up. A reader who expects a decision note to lead with the decision could treat the order as delay, but the definition says answer position alone is not a defect.

The text explicitly puts the answer after the working: "The working comes first". However, that working supplies the staff-mediated versus total transaction distinction, the hourly rates, and the per-person capacity. The staffing answer cannot be read correctly without them, so this counts as meaningful methodology rather than burial. A stricter reading could still object that a summary was available up front.

There is a competing reading. The Background section is short and is required by the template, and the Decision still arrives fairly early. On the other side, the template history, the booking and invoice details, the purchase history, and the generic explanation of hood machines add nothing to interpreting the schedule. The reasons that matter (cup counts, noise, staffing) come only after the decision.

The early line "two people at the desk for the whole day" could be read as an early summary that satisfies the answer requirement. However, the text defines the task as names against times and says a general plan would not help. That operative rota is held back behind the comments on the session and the branch's Saturday history, so the early phrase works as a teaser.

The method arrives after four paragraphs. These paragraphs separate warping from center cracking, cover the humidity logs and the canvas grip, and explain why the first fixes failed. They are causal explanation that each step relies on: the sliding surface, the shelves away from the grille, and leaving the panels unweighted. The text says it is settling this distinction first, so this reads as necessary setup. The short Theo 2019 aside is too small to count as burial.

The 172 mm order comes in the fourth paragraph. Before it, the text settles the cross pattern, which changes the length by about 13 mm and overrides the customer's request, and corrects the flange and ERD inputs. These are prerequisites the answer depends on, not unnecessary run-up. A stricter reading could say the order figure should come first, but under the definition the setup is needed.

The detour is a single paragraph of generic optics background that the question already took for granted. It delays the recommendation and adds nothing to how the reader understands it. Because it is so short, one could call it local unnecessary framing instead. It is substantive background, though, not an empty wrapper.

The connector advice may be useful for the repair overall. Still, it has nothing to do with the spoke-length question and contributes nothing to interpreting the lengths. It sits between the question and the answer, and the text itself marks it as coming 'before the numbers'.

The method appears in the fourth paragraph. Two readings compete. Read as setup, the first three paragraphs give necessary reasoning (lead paint, fine fibre dust, a hallway with no window) that explains why there's no sanding and no fan, and why the advice is containment plus filtration. Read as burial, the operative steps arrive late. I chose the setup reading because the earlier material shapes the instructions directly.

The proposed order comes after the log analysis, the site measurements and the contract terms. Each of those directly fixes the order: the loading bay blocking, the 3.2 m arch, the square clearing at 7pm, the defrost and collection terms. That makes it a necessary prerequisite, not unnecessary run-up. A competing reading is that a briefing should lead with its recommendation.

The site measurements and timing tests could be read as meaningful methodology. However, the order rests on the contract windows, and almost nothing from the interviews, questionnaire, measurements or spreadsheet is used to justify it.

The paragraph on transfer history (tape stock, sticky-shed baking, capture format, azimuth) adds little to how the level answer should be read. The one relevant fact, that recording levels varied, is given later with the answer itself. The tape history could also be read as useful context about the material.

The note says its template requires a Background section, which could justify putting the background first. However, the template history, the booking and invoice details, and the general explanation of how hood machines work add almost nothing to understanding the schedule, and they delay the Decision section. The canopy noise that matters to the reasoning is explained separately later in the note.

The early 'short version' (two people all day) could count as an early summary. But the request was for the hour-by-hour rota of named staff, and that rota is held back behind workshop praise and branch history. A short answer phrase near the start does not excuse delaying the actual answer.

The staffing answer comes after several paragraphs, but those paragraphs separate kiosk transactions from staff-handled ones and work out hourly demand and capacity. That is methodology needed to understand the answer, and the text says why it comes first. Someone could argue that the bottom line should come first, but under the definition, the answer's position alone does not count as a defect.

The Decision section comes after three sections: machine throughput, what has to be clean by when, and the windows when the machine cannot run. Each one supplies a constraint the block schedule depends on, so this is necessary setup, not padding. One could still argue that a decision note should open with the decision.

Two readings are possible. In the one I chose, the option-by-option tests (dryers, air drying, keeping the jackets dry, duplicates) are elimination reasoning. That reasoning explains why the recommendation is jackets-only duplicates plus tumble-drying, so it is meaningful methodology. In the other reading, a recommendation memo is expected to lead with its recommendation, so the test results come too early. I rejected that reading because the definition says an answer's position alone establishes no defect.

The last background sentence, which separates catalog-only changes from row rewrites, ties loosely to the answer. But the setup paragraph already covers that distinction for these two specific changes, so the generic definitions still delay the answer without helping interpret it.
The Monday levain advice is a real secondary help, not filler. Even so, it has nothing to do with the stated staggering question and sits ahead of the stagger answer.

The answer that the washer needs no repair comes late. However, the diagnostic tests, the fault log and the reproduction all support that answer, so this reads as necessary causal reasoning and meaningful methodology, not unnecessary run-up. The early line "The pump looks healthy" also signals the direction of the answer.

There are two readings. The RPD scoring could be necessary background for why the duplicate should be taken at the same spot and time. But the reporting limits, the absolute-difference rule, the MC-2 copper history and the D3 qualifier play no part in the spacing answer. The later explanation of the reasoning does not use them either. The delay is one paragraph.

The Background section's last sentence, which separates polar alignment from star alignment, gives some context for the recommendation. The rest of the section explains basic mounts and their history to a committee that the briefing itself says has already polar-aligned equatorial mounts. That material holds back the recommendation.

The rotor-rub paragraph could be read as an off-topic digression in a field plan rather than a run-up. However, it sits between the stated shifting question and the procedure, and it adds nothing to how the reader interprets the indexing answer.

The decision only arrives after long sections on the link, the tests and the codec. Read in terms of position alone, that could look like burial. But each section feeds directly into the slot choice: the congestion windows, the tide-linked bursts and the limits on burst tolerance. The note also says up front why it is ordered this way.

The early 'In brief' summary could be read as an early answer, but it skips both questions asked (folded vs opened, what goes between the faces). Those answers stay held back behind collection history, team history, general transport risks and logistics.

One reading: the paragraph about testing consolidation during the closure does relate to the closure, because it explains why the temporary stop should not be treated as a trial. Even so, the stop-spacing history, the delivery-van reliability issue and the scheduling correspondence don't help explain where the stop goes, and they hold back the recommendation until Section 2.

The recommendation comes late, but the note says up front why it presents the evidence first. The Calder Road evidence produces the three conditions that rule out the contractor's site and support the chosen one, so the run-up is necessary causal explanation rather than padding.

The $100 purchase-approval rule could be read as slightly relevant to buying the controller. But the $84 price is under that threshold, and the other preliminary material (agreement renewal, change of coordinator, donation history, regional trends) does nothing to help interpret the recommendation.

One reading treats the timber-movement and finish paragraphs as ruling out the wood as the cause before naming the fixings. The text never draws that link, though. The paragraphs are generic background, and the diagnosis and fix stand without them.
The run-up is only one paragraph, so one could call it a short digression rather than burial. Still, it is unrelated reminiscence placed between the question and its answer.

The line "The answer depends on which part is failing" defers the recommendation. The diagnosis that follows is necessary causal reasoning for repair versus replacement, so this is relevant setup, not an unnecessary run-up.

The run-up is only one paragraph. Someone could read it as implicitly ruling out flour, slicer, and dough causes, which would make it meaningful methodology. But the text never draws that conclusion, so the paragraph adds nothing to how the answer is understood.

The paragraph on compressor oil could be read as a quick check that the move caused no damage. But the reader says the fridge cools perfectly well, and the writer admits it is a favourite topic rather than part of the answer, so it mainly delays the diagnosis.

There are two readings. On one, the opening line about pixels per inch versus megapixels answers early enough, and the definitions of megapixels and dpi are useful prerequisites. On the other, the actual answer (300 ppi, 1820 by 2550 pixels) is held back behind a 'back to basics' paragraph of generic background like the origin of the word 'pixel'. The delay is only one short paragraph.

One reading treats the Maillard and combi-fan paragraphs as causal explanation behind the plan, since the uneven browning across trays could explain splitting the batches. The other reading, which I chose, is that this background is general roasting chemistry. It doesn't support the holding plan, which depends on steam trapping and staggered batches, and it only delays the plan.

The answer (valley overshoot) comes only in the Recommendation section. However, the material before it is needed to read that answer: it separates three kinds of overflow the residents' reports could describe, and it gives the hose test, camera, storm footage and capacity check that rule out the other two. One could argue a service recommendation should lead with its conclusion, but under the definition this is meaningful methodology, not unnecessary run-up.

The opening already narrows the cause to outlet backup ("Something at or below that outlet is not letting water away"), so it could be read as an adequate early summary. But the question asks which part of the drainage is at fault. The operative answer, the root-blocked buried drain line, only comes after generic background on gutter history, profiles and cleaning that adds nothing to reading it.

The routing answer arrives only at "So: do not leave either piece...". The paragraphs before it, though, are needed reasoning: they separate the fallback loop from the alert inserter, correct the power-cut date and work out the 101-hour gap, and the answer depends on each of these. This is purposeful setup, not filler.

The paper-stock run-up is only one paragraph and gives practical advice, so it could be read as a side note rather than burial. However, it has nothing to do with how the boards are moved, and the teaser holds back the plan until after it.

The early 'short version' (keep the length comparison, use the new clamp stands) partly answers the question, so one reading treats it as a sufficient early summary. But the task Dr Keane set is the lengths, release angle and timing method, and those come only after the history, personal reminiscence, purpose discussion and forum survey, none of which shapes the setup.

One reading treats the data collection and consultation as meaningful methodology. But the decision rests only on the Corran's gangway gradient and the safety management system limit, so the logged timings, crew views, other ports' practice and poll add little to how the answer should be read.

One reading treats this as a multi-finding site-visit report, where the former, retarder and flour sections are legitimate separate findings, and the flour question was also asked. The title and stated question are about the mixer schedule, though, and the report explicitly puts that answer after them ("Before the schedule").
